456.title: She loved much (Luke 7:36–50)
456.hook: a sinful woman washes his feet with tears at a dinner she wasn't invited to
456.howItsDone: Catholics connect this story with the sacrament of Penance, where sins are forgiven and the priest sends the penitent away in peace, and some pray with it as an examination of how much they have been forgiven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the gate of Naim, Jesus saw a grieving widow before anyone asked. Your line was weep not. A new week starts.

A dinner party in a nice house. The host is a Pharisee named Simon, who has asked the new teacher everyone is talking about to eat with him. The guests aren't on chairs; they recline on couches, leaning on one elbow, feet stretched out behind them. And someone comes in who was never asked: a woman of the city, known as a sinner, carrying an alabaster jar of ointment. She goes straight to the teacher's feet.
screen: `A DINNER AT SIMON'S HOUSE.` → `GUESTS RECLINING, FEET BEHIND.` → `AN UNINVITED WOMAN WITH A JAR.`

segments.voice: She stands behind him and starts to cry. Her tears fall on his feet, so she wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours out the ointment. Simon thinks: if this man were a prophet, he'd know what sort of woman is touching him. Jesus answers the thought with a story. Two men owe a lender money, one five hundred pence, one fifty. Neither can pay, so he forgives them both. Which will love him more? Simon answers carefully: I suppose the one forgiven more. Right, says Jesus. Then he turns toward the woman but keeps talking to Simon. You gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with tears. You gave me no kiss; she hasn't stopped kissing my feet. You didn't anoint my head; she anointed my feet. Then the line: "Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, he loveth less." To her he says: "Thy faith hath made thee safe, go in peace." Simon isn't the villain here. He invited Jesus, listened, and answered honestly. The story is about two kinds of guests, and it asks which one we are. Luke never names the woman. For many centuries in the Western Church, following a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great, she was identified with Mary Magdalene. The Church's calendar today no longer joins them, and the Gospel itself never says. What Luke does say is that she loved much, and that Jesus sent her away forgiven, in peace.

Then think of one person you've been loving carefully, in measured amounts, keeping track, and picture giving them one thing without counting: a kindness, an apology, an hour. If you pray, thank God for what you've been forgiven.

457.title: The women who funded him (Luke 8:1–3)
457.hook: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others ministered to him of their substance
457.howItsDone: The Church keeps the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on July 22, and in many Catholic parishes women carry much of the daily work: catechesis, sacristy care, charity, music and administration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an alabaster jar at Simon's dinner, and a woman who loved much. Your line was go in peace.

Here's a question the Gospels rarely stop to answer: who paid for all this? Jesus and twelve men walking from town to town for months, not fishing, not farming, not working for wages. Somebody bought the bread, the sandals, the oil, a roof when there was one. Most of the time the Gospels skip the budget. Luke doesn't. In three short verses, tucked between bigger stories, he tells us who kept the whole mission going.
screen: `WHO PAID FOR ALL THIS?` → `THIRTEEN MEN, NO WAGES.` → `THREE VERSES WITH THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Jesus went through the cities and towns preaching the kingdom, Luke says, and the twelve were with him, and certain women. Then he names them. Mary, called Magdalene, out of whom seven devils had gone. Joanna, wife of Chusa, Herod's steward: married to the man who managed the household of the king who would later mock Jesus. Susanna, about whom we know nothing else at all. And "many others who ministered unto him of their substance." Their substance means their own money and goods. These women weren't just along for the ride. They were paying for it. Ministered is worth stopping on. In Greek it's diakoneo, to serve, the same root that gives the Church the word deacon. Now follow these women forward. Luke says the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance and watched the crucifixion, and saw where he was laid. On Sunday morning, Mary Magdalene and Joanna are named among the women who found the tomb empty and told the apostles. The ones who funded the road were still there at the end. In 2016 Pope Francis raised the memorial of Mary Magdalene to a feast, and the decree honored her with an old title: apostle to the apostles. Many parishes still run on people like Joanna and Susanna, often women, often unnamed: the ones who count the collection, wash the linens, teach the children, bring the casseroles. Luke wrote their names down.

458.title: Take nothing (Luke 9:1–17)
458.hook: the twelve sent out light, then five thousand fed
458.howItsDone: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand from Luke on the solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ in the year of Luke's Gospel, and some religious orders vowed to poverty take the mission of the twelve as part of their pattern of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene and the women who paid for the road and stayed to the end. Your line was they ministered of their substance.

The charger, the spare charger, the snacks, the just-in-case jacket, the bag that won't close. That's packing for a weekend. Now take a mission instead: go to towns you've never seen, heal the sick, preach the kingdom of God. The packing list comes back mostly crossed out. That's chapter nine of Luke. The twelve are sent out on their own, and when they come back, there's a hungry crowd of thousands and almost no food.
screen: `THE BAG THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `A PACKING LIST, CROSSED OUT.` → `TWO SCENES ABOUT HAVING NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Jesus gives the twelve power over devils and diseases, and then the list: "Take nothing for your journey; neither staff, nor scrip, nor bread, nor money; neither have two coats." A scrip is a traveler's bag, the kind you'd carry food in. Stay in whatever house takes you in. If a town won't receive you, shake the dust off your feet and move on. Why so little? Luke doesn't say. One way to read it: traveling light means depending on others. The twelve have to knock on doors and be received; their poverty makes room for someone else's welcome. And it works: they go through the towns preaching and healing everywhere. When they come back, Jesus takes them aside to a desert place near Bethsaida, and the crowds follow. Evening comes. The twelve suggest the practical thing: send them away to find food and lodging. Jesus answers: "Give you them to eat." They count what they have: five loaves and two fishes, and about five thousand men. Here Luke slows down. Jesus takes the bread, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives to the disciples to set before the crowd. Took, blessed, broke, gave. Catholics hear nearly the same movements at every Mass, in the words of the Last Supper. Everyone eats and is filled, and twelve baskets of fragments are gathered up, from what the twelve had called too little. First they learn to go out with nothing. Then they learn that what little they have, placed in his hands, is enough to feed a crowd.

459.title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
459.hook: he turns toward Jerusalem, and the foxes have holes
459.howItsDone: Catholics hear this passage at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel; the Catechism teaches that family ties matter but are not absolute, and that following Jesus comes first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve sent out with nothing, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was nothing for the journey.

Partway through Luke's Gospel, the book turns. Until now Jesus has moved around Galilee: the lake, the villages, the hills. Then, in one verse, he turns toward Jerusalem, the city where, as he has already told his disciples, he will suffer. From here on, Luke tells the story as one long walk. Readers call this stretch the travel narrative. And the very first thing that happens on the road is a door shut in his face.
screen: `IN ONE VERSE, THE BOOK TURNS.` → `ONE LONG WALK TO JERUSALEM.` → `A DOOR SHUTS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the hinge in the Douay-Rheims: "And it came to pass, when the days of his assumption were accomplishing, that he steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." Assumption here means his being taken up, to the cross and to the Father. To set your face is an old Hebrew way of speaking: fix your direction and refuse to be turned. Isaiah's servant says he has set his face hard as rock. Jesus sends messengers ahead into a Samaritan village, and the village won't receive him, because he's headed for Jerusalem. James and John ask if they should call fire down from heaven. Jesus rebukes them, and they simply go on to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you wherever you go. Jesus answers: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Know what you're signing up for. The second says, let me first go and bury my father. The third, let me first say goodbye at home. Jesus answers with a farmer's picture: "No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." Look over your shoulder, and the furrow wanders. Luke doesn't soften these sayings. The Church reads them not as contempt for family, which the commandments honor, but as a question of what comes first. Jesus has set his face. He asks the people walking beside him to set theirs.

Picture yourself turning your face toward it, the way you'd turn to walk a road, and notice the urge to look back without obeying it. If you pray, ask for steadiness.

460.title: The seventy-two (Luke 10:1–24)
460.hook: sent in pairs like lambs among wolves, peace to this house
460.howItsDone: Some Catholic families bless their homes at Epiphany by chalking the year and the letters C+M+B over the door, and the traditional rite for blessing a house opens with Jesus' words, peace be to this house.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem, and the foxes had holes. Your line was no looking back.

Around the Epiphany in January, in some Catholic homes, someone climbs on a chair with a piece of blessed chalk and writes over the front door: the year, split in two, with three letters in the middle, C, M and B, joined by crosses. People read the letters as the names tradition gives the three wise men, and also as the start of a Latin blessing: may Christ bless this house. It's a small, homemade custom. The wish in it is much older: on a road in Luke, Jesus sends out a wider circle of disciples and tells them the first thing to say at every door.
screen: `CHALK OVER THE FRONT DOOR.` → `MAY CHRIST BLESS THIS HOUSE.` → `THE FIRST THING TO SAY AT A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Now he sends people ahead of him, and not just the twelve. The Douay-Rheims says the Lord appointed "other seventy-two: and he sent them two and two before his face into every city and place whither he himself was to come." Two and two, so nobody goes alone. Then the honest warning: "behold I send you as lambs among wolves." No purse, no bag, no sandals, no stopping to chat on the road. And at every door, one sentence first: "Into whatsoever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house." If a son of peace is there, Jesus says, your peace will rest on him. If not, it will come back to you. A blessing can't be wasted: it lands, or it returns. Behind the Gospel's word for peace stands the Hebrew shalom: not just quiet, but wholeness, everything as it should be. The number is a small puzzle: some Bibles say seventy here, and the Douay says seventy-two. Some readers connect it with the list of the world's nations in Genesis chapter ten, and hear in it a message meant for everyone. And the ending is pure joy. The seventy-two come back thrilled: even the devils obey us! Jesus says rejoice in something better: your names are written in heaven.

461.title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–13)
461.hook: the Our Father, a friend at midnight, ask, seek, knock
461.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Our Father at every Mass and at the start of each decade of the rosary; the Catechism devotes its final section to the prayer, comparing Luke's five petitions with Matthew's seven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventy-two went out two by two with one sentence for every door. Your line was peace be to this house.

It's midnight. A friend has shown up after a long trip, hungry, and your kitchen is empty. Not a crust. So you walk next door and knock. From inside, your neighbor groans: the door's locked, the kids are asleep in the bed with me, I can't get up. You knock again. Jesus tells this little comedy as his answer to a request from his disciples.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, AN EMPTY KITCHEN.` → `THE KIDS ARE ASLEEP. GO AWAY.` → `YOU KNOCK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Jesus is praying somewhere, and when he stops, one of his disciples says: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." John had given his followers a way to pray. Now Jesus gives his. Luke's Our Father is shorter than Matthew's, the one Catholics say at Mass. The Catechism notes the difference: Luke gives five petitions, Matthew seven. Luke's begins simply with Father, then hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, give us our daily bread, forgive us our sins as we forgive, and lead us not into temptation. Then, right away, the midnight friend. Even if the neighbor won't get up because you're his friend, Jesus says, "yet, because of his importunity, he will rise, and give him as many as he needeth." Importunity means pestering. The Greek word is bolder: shamelessness. The man gets bread because he won't stop knocking. Then the promise: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you." And one last picture: which father, if his son asks for a fish, hands him a snake? If you, imperfect as you are, give good things to your children, how much more will the Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him. Notice where the promise ends: not with whatever you ask for, but with the good Spirit.

segments.voice: Think of something you asked for once and gave up on: healing for someone, a change in yourself, an answer that never came. Let it come back without embarrassment; the man at midnight wasn't embarrassed. If you pray, ask again, plainly, and ask for the good Spirit too; if you don't, hold the hope out once more, like a hand raised to knock.

462.title: Blessed the womb (Luke 11:27–28)
462.hook: a woman praises his mother; he says blessed are they who hear the word and keep it; Catholics see Mary as both
462.howItsDone: Catholics read Luke 11:27–28 on some feasts and Saturday Masses of Our Lady, and many pray the rosary as a way of pondering the Gospel's words with Mary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples asked to be taught to pray, and a man's importunity kept him knocking at midnight. Your line was knock.

A son gives a great speech at a wedding, and an aunt in the crowd calls out: your mother must be so proud! It's a compliment to him, routed through her. Something like that happens in Luke. Jesus is in the middle of a tense argument with people who say he heals by the power of devils. A woman in the crowd can't hold it in. She lifts up her voice and calls out a blessing on his mother. It's two verses long: what she said, and what he said back.
screen: `YOUR MOTHER MUST BE SO PROUD.` → `A VOICE FROM THE CROWD.` → `TWO VERSES LONG.`

segments.voice: Here's her cry in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the paps that gave thee suck." Paps is an old word for breasts. It's an earthy, motherly blessing, the kind women in that world gave: how happy the mother of such a son. Jesus answers: "Yea rather, blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it." Some people hear that as a brush-off of his mother. Catholics hear something else, and Luke gives the reason. When the angel came, Mary said be it done to me according to thy word. At Bethlehem, Luke says, Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. Elizabeth says to her, blessed art thou that hast believed. And in her own song, Mary says all generations shall call me blessed. So in Luke, Mary carries both blessings at once: she bore him, and she heard and kept the word. Augustine said it this way, in his own words: Mary was more blessed in receiving Christ by faith than in conceiving him in the flesh. Jesus takes a blessing only one woman in history could have, and opens it to everyone listening. Nobody else can be his mother. Anybody can hear and keep. That's why Catholics honor Mary as the first disciple, not only as a mother: she shows what keeping looks like.
screen: `BLESSED IS THE WOMB THAT BORE THEE.` · `YEA RATHER: HEAR AND KEEP.` · `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.` · `ONE COULD BEAR HIM; ALL CAN KEEP.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY WHO HEAR AND KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Let one of this week's lines choose you: go in peace, nothing for the journey, no looking back, peace be to this house, knock. Say it slowly inside a few times, the way Mary pondered, and don't analyze it; just keep it, like a stone in your pocket you keep touching. If you pray, ask to keep it the way she did.
Blessed the womb. A woman's cry from the crowd praising Jesus' mother, and his answer: blessed are those who hear the word and keep it, as Mary did. Today's word.

Your line: hear and keep it. That's week sixty-six: she loved much, the women who funded him, take nothing, he set his face, the seventy-two, teach us to pray, and the womb. Day four hundred sixty-two, in the books.

chat.says: Jesus said "blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it." Who's that about?
options: Anyone who hears and keeps it, and Mary first of all; she did both.
Only Mary, since she alone could bear him and be his mother.
Only the twelve apostles, who heard him teach every single day.
chat.meaning: Nobody else can be his mother, but anybody can hear and keep; Luke shows Mary doing both, so Catholics call her the first disciple.
